mainTopic: Confessing to a קנס: seduction and theft, and whether the half-damage of a תם ox is ממון or קנס
overview: The משנה teaches that a person who confesses pays real damages, like בושת ופגם or the stolen קרן, but never pays a קנס based on his own admission. The general rule is that any payment above the actual damage is a קנס, and a confession cannot make him pay it. The גמרא explains that the משנה chose seduction over rape because seduction is the bigger חידוש: even though his words tarnish the girl, he still pays. רבי שמעון disagrees and says he cannot tarnish her, so he pays nothing. Even if she, her father, and her family agree, some relative far away will always object. The גמרא then brings a dispute between רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע about whether the half-damage paid for a תם ox is ממון or קנס. Each view depends on whether ordinary oxen are assumed to be safe. The גמרא tests this with a משנה about the damaged party sharing in the payment and with a ברייתא listing the differences between תם and מועד. The discussion of whether חצי כופר counts as something the list left out continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Confessing to seduction or theft: regular damages yes, fine no
steps.stepSummary: A man who admits he seduced a girl pays בושת ופגם but not the קנס. A man who admits he stole pays the קרן but not כפל or ארבעה וחמשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'I seduced so-and-so's daughter,' he pays for embarrassment and damage on his own word, but not the fine. If someone says 'I stole,' he pays back what he took, but not double or four-and-five times.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with two cases where a man's own confession makes him pay the normal damages but not the extra fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בושת and פגם pay for real harm, so a confession is enough. The קנס of seduction, and the extra payments of כפל and ארבעה וחמשה, go beyond the real loss. A person cannot obligate himself in those just by confessing.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for embarrassment and for the loss in her value
A fixed fine set by the Torah, beyond the actual damage
The principal, the actual value of what was stolen
The double payment a thief owes

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who says:
'I seduced the daughter of so-and-so'
pays for humiliation and degradation
based on his own admission,
but does not pay the fine.
One who says: 'I stole'

phrases.aramaic: — מְשַׁלֵּם אֶת הַקֶּרֶן עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: pays the principal based on his own admission,
but does not pay the double payment
or the payment of four and five.
phrases.notes: This is what a thief pays if he slaughtered or sold the stolen sheep (four times) or ox (five times).

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Confession obligates real damages (בושת ופגם, קרן) but not a קנס or punitive payments.

steps.title: The ox cases and the general rule
steps.stepSummary: Admitting your ox killed a person or another ox makes you pay. Admitting it killed a slave does not, because that payment is a fixed fine. Rule: whatever is more than the damage is not paid on your own word.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'my ox killed so-and-so' or 'so-and-so's ox,' he pays on his own word. If he says 'my ox killed so-and-so's slave,' he doesn't. The rule: anyone who pays more than he damaged does not pay on his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds the ox cases and then sums everything up with one general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying for a person or an ox is paying for real damage, so a confession works. The 30 shekels for a slave is a fixed amount no matter what the slave was worth, so it counts as a קנס. The כלל ties all the cases together: extra payment equals קנס, and a קנס needs witnesses.
steps.whatToRemember: Any payment above the actual damage is a קנס, and a person never pays a קנס based on his own confession.

phrases.english: 'My ox killed so-and-so,'
or 'the ox of so-and-so'

phrases.aramaic: — הֲרֵי זֶה מְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: this one pays based on his own admission.
'My ox killed the slave of so-and-so'
he does not pay based on his own admission.
phrases.notes: The payment for a slave is a set 30 shekels whatever he was worth, so it counts as a fine.

phrases.english: This is the principle:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַמְשַׁלֵּם יָתֵר עַל מַה שֶּׁהִזִּיק
phrases.english: anyone who pays more than what he damaged
does not pay based on his own admission.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל הַמְשַׁלֵּם יָתֵר עַל מַה שֶּׁהִזִּיק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Payments beyond actual damage (like the slave's fixed amount) are קנס and are not paid on one's own admission.

steps.title: Why not use the case of rape?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה says 'I seduced' instead of 'I raped'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the משנה teach the case of 'I raped her'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the משנה: it could have used the case of אונס, so why did it pick פיתוי?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אונס and פיתוי carry a קנס plus בושת ופגם, so either case could show the rule. The גמרא wants to know what the choice of פיתוי is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: And let it teach (why didn't it say)

phrases.english: GEMARA: But let it teach 'I raped'!

steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's choice of the seduction case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rape case has the same payments, so why not mention it?

steps.title: Seduction is the bigger חידוש
steps.stepSummary: With אונס it is obvious that he pays on his own word. With פיתוי he is tarnishing her too, so you might think he isn't believed. The משנה teaches that he still pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is saying 'no need to say.' No need to say 'I raped,' where he doesn't tarnish her, that he pays on his own word. But with 'I seduced,' where he does tarnish her, you might say he doesn't pay on his own word. So it teaches us that he does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה chose the harder case on purpose, to teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I raped her' only blames himself. Saying 'I seduced her' also says she agreed, which damages her name, so you might think we ignore his words entirely. The משנה teaches that he still pays בושת ופגם.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary to say

phrases.english: It is saying 'it is not necessary':
It is not necessary to say 'I raped,'
where he does not tarnish her,
phrases.notes: If she was forced, she did nothing wrong, so her name is not hurt.

phrases.aramaic: דִּמְשַׁלֵּם בּוֹשֶׁת וּפְגָם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: that he pays humiliation and degradation on his own admission,
but 'I seduced,' where he does tarnish her,

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא: לָא מְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
phrases.english: I might say: he does not pay on his own admission
so it teaches us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the משנה's wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: לא מבעיא: the משנה chose the bigger חידוש
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because he tarnishes her, his confession might be thrown out completely.
steps.terutzMaskana: He still pays בושת ופגם on his own admission even in seduction.

steps.title: רבי שמעון disagrees: he cannot tarnish her
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי שמעון saying that the seducer doesn't even pay בושת ופגם on his own word, because he has no power to tarnish another man's daughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה is not like this תנא, as it was taught: רבי שמעון בן יהודה says in the name of רבי שמעון: even בושת ופגם he does not pay on his own word, since he has no power to tarnish so-and-so's daughter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the ruling of our משנה is not unanimous and brings a ברייתא with the opposing view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'you might think' from the last step is really רבי שמעון's position. In his view, a confession that ruins her name is rejected entirely, so he pays nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (in a ברייתא)
A sage of the משנה period
It is not in his power

phrases.english: Our mishna is not in accordance with this tanna,

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
phrases.english: as it is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says
in the name of Rabbi Shimon:
even humiliation and degradation
he does not pay based on his own admission
it is not within his power
to tarnish the daughter of so-and-so.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון, a confession of seduction does not obligate even בושת ופגם, since he cannot damage her reputation.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the 'might have thought' in the previous step is a real opinion held by a תנא.

steps.title: What if the girl herself agrees?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי: according to רבי שמעון, what if she agrees with his story?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: if she herself is fine with it, what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא probes רבי שמעון's reason: if the problem is hurting her, what if she admits it herself?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she agrees, nobody seems to be hurt by his words, so maybe he should pay. This is the first of three similar questions.

keyTerms.meaning: It is acceptable to her, she agrees

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
If she herself is agreeable, what is the law?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does her own agreement allow his confession to count according to רבי שמעון?

steps.title: Her father may object
steps.stepSummary: The answer: her father might not agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe her father doesn't agree.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that her agreeing isn't enough, because the shame affects her father too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The damage to her name is not only hers. Her father's honor is also on the line, so her consent alone doesn't solve the problem.

phrases.english: Perhaps her father is not agreeable.
phrases.notes: The text doesn't say who answers here; it is אביי replying to רב פפא.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Her father's honor is also hurt, so her consent is not enough.

steps.title: What if her father also agrees?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא pushes further: what if the father agrees too?
steps.simpleTranslation: If her father is fine with it, what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks the next step up: what if both she and her father agree?
steps.deeperAnalysis: He removes the objection that was just raised to see whether anything else still stands in the way.

phrases.english: If her father is agreeable, what is the law?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the father's consent make the confession count?

steps.title: The family may object
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the rest of the family might not agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe the family members don't agree.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that the shame reaches the whole family, not just the father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stain on her name affects all her relatives, so the father's consent still doesn't cover everyone who is harmed.

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא לָא נִיחָא לְהוּ לִבְנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה.
phrases.english: Perhaps the family members are not agreeable.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא לָא נִיחָא לְהוּ לִבְנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The whole family is shamed, so the father's consent is not enough.

steps.title: What if the whole family agrees?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks one last time: what if the family members agree too?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the family members are fine with it, what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא makes his final push: what if everyone in the family agrees?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the strongest form of the question. If every known relative agrees, there seems to be no one left who is hurt.

phrases.english: If the family members are agreeable, what is the law?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the consent of all the family members make the confession count?

steps.title: There's always one relative overseas who objects
steps.stepSummary: It is impossible that there isn't some relative far away who doesn't agree, so according to רבי שמעון the confession never counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: It's impossible that there isn't one relative overseas who isn't fine with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer closes the discussion: you can never get everyone's agreement, so his confession can never tarnish her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the shame reaches relatives everywhere, there will always be someone who did not agree. So according to רבי שמעון, consent never makes his confession work.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, a man's confession of seduction never counts, not even with the consent of the girl, her father, or her local family, because some distant relative will always object.

phrases.english: It is impossible that there is not one
in a country overseas who is not agreeable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלֵיכָּא חַד בִּמְדִינַת הַיָּם
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רבי שמעון, no amount of consent lets the seducer's confession tarnish the girl, since some relative will always object.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: one who admits stealing pays only the principal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: someone who admits 'I stole' pays only what he took.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who says, 'I stole,' pays back the principal, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה to open a new topic. This step sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra payments for a thief (double, or four and five times) are a קנס. A person who admits on his own to something that carries a קנס does not pay the קנס, so he pays only the קרן (principal).

keyTerms.meaning: the principal, meaning the actual value that was taken
and so on (the rest of the line of the משנה)

phrases.english: One who says: I stole
pays the principal, etc.
phrases.notes: The full line goes on to say he doesn't pay the double payment or the four-and-five payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the רבי שמעון discussion to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Admitting to theft obligates only the principal, not the extra payments.

steps.title: The dispute: is half-damage money or a fine?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says half-damage is ממון, and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says it is קנס.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated about half-damage: רב פפא said half-damage is money (repayment). רב הונא son of רב יהושע said half-damage is a fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an argument between two אמוראים about the half-damage payment for an ox that is not yet known to gore (a תם).
steps.deeperAnalysis: If half-damage is ממון, it is real repayment for a loss. If it is קנס, it is a penalty, and the rules of a קנס, such as being exempt after admitting it yourself, would apply. That ties the argument back to our משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: it was stated (introduces an argument between אמוראים)
half-damage, paid when a תם ox gores
money, meaning true repayment for a loss

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree on how much is paid (half). They argue only about what kind of payment it is.

phrases.english: It was stated: half-damage,
phrases.notes: This is the half payment owed when an ox that hasn't gored three times yet gores.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
half-damage is money.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said:
half-damage is a fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a related קנס question that comes out of the משנה's rule about admitting to a fine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא: half-damage is ממון. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: half-damage is קנס.

steps.title: רב פפא's reasoning: oxen are not assumed safe
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא holds that ordinary oxen are not assumed to be tame, so really the owner should pay everything, and the תורה gave him a break.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said half-damage is money because he holds that ordinary oxen are not assumed to be safe. By right the owner should pay all of it, but the תורה had pity on him because the ox has not yet been warned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב פפא calls half-damage ממון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since an ordinary ox may well gore, the owner is truly responsible for the full loss. Paying half is a discount the תורה gives because the ox is still a תם. So whatever he does pay is real repayment.

keyTerms.meaning: assumed to be safe or tame
the Merciful One, meaning the תורה
was warned, meaning it became a מועד (known to gore)

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא מָמוֹנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said half-damage is money,
because he holds: ordinary oxen
are not assumed to be safe.
And by right he should pay all of it,
and it is the Merciful One who has pity on him,
because the ox has not yet been warned.
phrases.notes: He means the ox hasn't gored three times yet, so it isn't known as a goring ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא מָמוֹנָא, קָסָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the first opinion in the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oxen are not assumed safe, so full liability is the basic rule and half is a discount. Therefore the payment is ממון.

steps.title: רב הונא's reasoning: oxen are assumed safe
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע holds that ordinary oxen are assumed tame, so really the owner should pay nothing, and the תורה fined him so he would guard his ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said half-damage is a fine because he holds that ordinary oxen are assumed to be safe. By right he should pay nothing at all, but the תורה fined him so that he will guard his ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב הונא calls half-damage קנס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If oxen are normally tame, the owner could not have expected the goring, so he owes nothing by basic law. The half payment is an extra penalty to push owners to watch their animals, and that makes it a קנס.

keyTerms.meaning: by right, by the basic law

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions depend on one question: are ordinary oxen assumed safe? If not, half-damage is a discount on a real debt (ממון). If they are, half-damage is an added penalty (קנס).

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא קְנָסָא,
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said half-damage is a fine,
because he holds: ordinary oxen
are assumed to be safe.
And by right he should not pay at all,
and it is the Merciful One who fined him,
so that he will guard his ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא קְנָסָא, קָסָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for the second opinion, the opposite of רב פפא's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oxen are assumed safe, so there is no basic liability, and the half payment is a penalty. Therefore it is קנס.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming proofs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a list of key words to help remember the order of the proofs that come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: A memory aid: damaged, what, and killed, principle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is giving a memory aid, made of short code words. It is setting up a series of challenges that are about to come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word points to a key word in one of the upcoming proofs. The first one, 'damaged,' hints at the next proof about 'the damaged one and the damager.'

keyTerms.meaning: a memory aid, a short list of key words

phrases.english: Memory aid: damaged, what, and killed, principle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prepares the list of proofs and challenges about the dispute.

steps.title: Challenge: how can the damaged party 'share in the payment' if it's a fine?
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says the damaged party and the damager share in the payment. That fits ממון, but under קנס the damaged party only gains, so how is he 'paying'?
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: the damaged party and the damager share in the payment. That works well for the one who says half-damage is money, because then the damaged party really does share the loss. But for the one who says it is a fine, he is taking something that isn't really his. How can he be called a sharer in the payment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses a משנה to challenge רב הונא, who holds that half-damage is קנס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If half-damage is ממון, the victim was owed everything and loses half, so he really shares the cost. If it is קנס, the victim was owed nothing and receives half as a gift. A person who only gains is not 'paying' anything.

keyTerms.meaning: the damaged party and the one who caused the damage
it makes sense (for one view, before a 'but' for the other)

phrases.english: We learned: the damaged party and the damager share in the payment.
It makes sense according to the one who says
half-damage is money,
that is how the damaged party has a share in the payment.
phrases.notes: He was owed the whole amount and only gets half, so he is covering part of the loss himself.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא קְנָסָא,
phrases.english: But according to the one who says half-damage is a fine,
now that he is taking what isn't his,
is he sharing in the payment?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first proof listed in the memory aid ('damaged').
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's view that half-damage is קנס
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under קנס the victim only gains, so the משנה's words that he 'shares in the payment' do not fit.

steps.title: Answer: the משנה is talking about the carcass losing value
steps.stepSummary: The 'sharing' the משנה means is that the victim takes the loss when the dead animal's value drops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was only needed for the drop in the carcass's value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the קנס view by explaining the משנה's words in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim's 'share in the payment' is not about the half-damage at all. It means he has to absorb the loss if the dead animal becomes worth less before he sells it. So even under קנס he really does lose something.

keyTerms.meaning: it was only needed for (narrows a statement to a specific case)
the drop in value of the dead animal's carcass

phrases.english: It was needed only for the drop in the carcass's value.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the משנה's phrase to refer to a different loss
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Sharing in the payment' meant losing part of the half-damage, which works only for ממון.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Sharing' means taking the loss of the carcass's value, which works even for קנס.

steps.title: Challenge: the carcass rule was already taught
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא already teaches that the owners deal with the carcass, so why would the משנה need to repeat it?
steps.simpleTranslation: The drop in the carcass's value? We already learned it: 'payments of damage' teaches that the owners take care of the carcass!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave, because the carcass rule is already known from another source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the words 'payments of damage' already teach that the victim bears the carcass's loss in value, then the משנה's phrase 'share in the payment' would be repeating something we know. So reading it as the carcass rule seems unnecessary, and the challenge against קנס comes back.

phrases.english: The drop in the carcass's value? We already learned it:
'Payments of damage'
teaches that the owners take care of the carcass!
phrases.notes: So the owner of the dead animal is the one who bears any drop in its value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that 'share in the payment' refers to פחת נבילה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The carcass rule is already taught by 'payments of damage', so the משנה would be repeating it for no reason.

steps.title: One source is about a תם ox and one about a מועד ox
steps.stepSummary: The משנה and the ברייתא are not repeating each other. One teaches the rule for a תם ox and the other for a מועד ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: One is about an innocent ox, and one is about a warned ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 19: why would the משנה repeat what the ברייתא already teaches? The answer is that each source is talking about a different kind of ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that the victim takes the loss when the carcass drops in value appears twice. That is because one place is about a תם and the other is about a מועד. So nothing is repeated, and the explanation from Step 18 can stand.

keyTerms.meaning: An 'innocent' ox that has not yet gored three times. Its owner pays half the damage.
A 'warned' ox that has gored three times. Its owner pays the full damage.

phrases.english: One is about an innocent ox, and one is about a warned ox.
phrases.notes: 'One' means one of the two sources, either the משנה or the ברייתא from Step 19.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of repetition from Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting cases: each source covers a different type of ox.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources teach the same rule about the same ox, so one of them is extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: One source covers a תם and the other covers a מועד, so neither one is extra.

steps.title: Why both cases had to be taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows why we could not learn the מועד case from the תם case, or the תם case from the מועד case.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both are needed. If it had taught us only the innocent ox, I would say the reason is that it was not yet warned, but a warned ox that was warned, I would say no. And if it had taught us only the warned ox, I would say the reason is that he pays the whole damage, but an innocent ox, I would say no. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer by showing that each case teaches something the other could not. This is the classic 'צריכא' move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a תם, we might go easy on the owner because his ox was never warned. That reason does not apply to a מועד. For a מועד, we might ignore the small drop in the carcass's value because the owner already pays everything. That reason does not apply to a תם, whose owner pays only half. Since the two reasons are different, both cases must be written.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed: both teachings are necessary
I would say no (the rule would not apply)

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that the victim takes the loss when the carcass drops in value applies to both a תם and a מועד. Each one needed its own source, so the explanation from Step 18 holds up.

phrases.english: And both are needed, for if it had taught us only an innocent ox:
I would say the reason is that it was not yet warned,
but a warned ox, which was warned, I would say no.
And if it had taught us only a warned ox:
I would say the reason is that he pays the whole damage,
but an innocent ox, I would say no.
So both are needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in Step 20 by showing that each case is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא: each case has its own reason for leniency that does not carry over to the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We could learn one case from the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each case has a different reason, so both had to be stated.

steps.title: A list of differences between תם and מועד leaves out 'own admission'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists how a תם differs from a מועד but does not mention paying based on one's own admission. This suggests half-damage is ממון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: What is the difference between an innocent ox and a warned ox? The innocent ox pays half the damage from its own body, and the warned ox pays full damage from the best property. It does not teach that the innocent ox's owner does not pay based on his own admission while the warned ox's owner does pay based on his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof that half-damage is real money (ממון) and not a fine (קנס).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fine is not paid when a person admits to it on his own. If half-damage were a קנס, the owner of a תם would not pay based on his own admission, while the owner of a מועד would. That would be a big difference between them. Since the ברייתא does not list it, it seems there is no such difference, so half-damage is ממון.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the opening for a proof
From its body: payment is collected only from the goring ox itself
From the best property: payment is collected from the owner's finest assets

steps.confusionAlert: The proof comes from what the ברייתא does NOT say. The missing difference is the evidence.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: מָה בֵּין תָּם לְמוּעָד,
phrases.english: Come and hear: What is the difference between an innocent ox and a warned ox?
That the innocent ox pays half the damage from its own body,
phrases.notes: If the goring ox is worth less than half the damage, the victim gets only what the ox is worth.

phrases.aramaic: וּמוּעָד מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם מִן הָעֲלִיָּיה.
phrases.english: and the warned ox pays full damage from the best property.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא קָתָנֵי שֶׁהַתָּם אֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: But it does not teach that the innocent ox does not pay based on his own admission,
and the warned ox pays based on his own admission.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מָה בֵּין תָּם לְמוּעָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the previous proof was turned away, the גמרא tries a new proof from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That half-damage is ממון, against רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע in Step 15, who called it a קנס.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of 'מה בין תם למועד', which leaves out any difference about paying based on one's own admission.

steps.title: The תנא left some things out
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away: the list is not complete, so the missing item proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He taught some and left some out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by saying the ברייתא's list was never meant to include every difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An argument from silence only works if the list is complete. If the תנא sometimes leaves things out, then leaving out 'own admission' may mean nothing, and half-damage could still be a קנס.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught and left out: the list is not complete

phrases.english: He taught some and left some out.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the ברייתא's silence.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the list is complete, but the תנא may have left items out.

steps.title: What else did he leave out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא demands a second missing item, since 'he left things out' only works if more than one thing is missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: What else did he leave out, that we should say he left this out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that the תנא left things out by asking for another example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of thumb is that you can only say 'he left things out' if there are at least two missing items. If only one thing is missing, it was probably left out on purpose.

phrases.english: What else did he leave out, that we should say he left this out?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'He left things out' needs at least one more missing item. Without one, the omission looks intentional.

steps.title: He also left out half-ransom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a second missing difference: חצי כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He left out half-ransom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by naming another difference between a תם and a מועד that the ברייתא does not list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a מועד kills a person, its owner pays כופר, but the owner of a תם does not pay even half a כופר. That difference is also missing from the list. So the list is not complete, and leaving out 'own admission' would prove nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom paid by the owner of an ox that killed a person
Half-ransom (the owner of a תם does not pay it)

phrases.english: He left out half-ransom.
phrases.notes: The owner of a תם ox that kills a person does not pay even half a ransom. That difference is not in the list either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 24 by giving a second missing item.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a second omission to show the list is not complete.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Own admission' is the only thing missing, so it was left out on purpose.
steps.terutzMaskana: חצי כופר is also missing, so the list is not complete.

steps.title: Half-ransom does not count as a missing item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: חצי כופר is not really something the list left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is because of half-ransom, that is not a real omission,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion that חצי כופר is a second missing item. The explanation of why continues right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חצי כופר does not count as something left out, then 'own admission' is still the only missing item. That would bring back the proof that half-damage is ממון. This sets up the next move.

phrases.english: If it is because of half-ransom,
that is not an omission,

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מִשּׁוּם חֲצִי כוֹפֶר לָאו שִׁיּוּרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer given in Step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The use of חצי כופר as a second missing item.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: חצי כופר is not truly something the list left out. The reason is given right after this line.
